catalog_quote: 2.8. Suprasegmentals. Accent is defined here as an abstract property of morphemes to be able to carry high pitch. The presence of accent is marked by ´ and is contrastive. ... The accent-bearing unit is the syllable, but, on long vowels, accent may fall either on the first or the second mora. ... Falling and rising tones, being predictable, are not marked in the transcription. Opposition between a falling and a rising tone may be seen in the Past vs. NonPast of verbal stems of shape CVVC (cf. 3.9.3). ... Accent may be lexically or morphologically defined, or may be assigned by default. In this case, it affects the penultimate syllable. Default-assigned accent is not marked in the phonological transcription. ... Penultimate position is the rule for accent placement also in plurimorphemic words resulting from the affixation/cliticization of accentless morphemes. ... Morphologically-assign…

audit.reasoning: The deciding quotation is verbatim in the open-access PDF we hold at the stated sections/pages (2.8 pp. 71-72; 2.10 p. 74; 3.9.3 pp. 94-95). The source is the standard and fullest description of Ongota, written by the language's principal fieldworkers, with an explicit analysis: contrastive 'accent' = ability to carry high pitch, lexically/morphologically assigned, default penult, word = accent domain, tense marked by accent placement. The authors' 2007 and 2015 statements (downloaded now, open access) restate the system as 'tonal accent' and confirm suprasegmental tense marking; the 2015 wording of the verbal rule (past = rightmost verb syllable, non-past = preceding syllable/clitic) could be added to the the primary-stress rule note but does not alter the tonal-OR-pitch accent classification or the penult default. sources.citation: Savà, Graziano & Mauro Tosco. 2015. The Ongota language – and two ways of looking at the history of the marginal and hunting-gathering peoples of East Africa. Ethnorêma 11: 1-17.
sources.quote: 'there are no person and tense verbal suffixes; expression of tense is based on tonal accent change. ... Tense is expressed by placing the tonal accent on the rightmost syllable of the verb, in which case the tense is past, or in the preceding one, in order to express non-past tense. The non-past position of the accent in monosyllabic verbs is on the pronominal clitic' (cata ka=cák 'I ate' vs cata ká=cak 'I eat/will eat'). Confirms a pitch/tonal-accent system with morphologically placed accent; the verbal rule is phrased as rightmost (past) vs preceding syllable (non-past) rather than 2000's '

sources.citation: Savà, Graziano & Mauro Tosco. 2007. Review article: Harold C. Fleming, Ongota: A Decisive Language in African Prehistory (Wiesbaden: Harrassowitz, 2006). Aethiopica 10: 223-232.
sources.quote: On Fleming 2006: 'the chapter treats phonology (pp. 24-26), some morphology (pp. 26-28 ...)' copied from Fleming et al. (1992). On Ongota: 'Ongota also lacks suffixal expression of tense. This is expressed by the displacement of the tonal accent along the verbal word, which, of course, includes the subject clitic. ... Suprasegmentally-marked tense is a piece of analysis found in Savà and Tosco (2000), a sketch of Ongota that Fleming did not include'.

tone.summary: Annotated oral text with IPA phonetic and phonemic tiers; says nothing about tone, pitch or accent and no Ongota form carries an accent or tone mark; '/' and '//' mark minor/major prosodic units only.
